newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK INSTITUTIONAL INVESTORS SEEK MARKET CHANGES.
newsitem.headline: GREEK INSTITUTIONAL INVESTORS SEEK MARKET CHANGES.

text.p: Seeking to raise dialogue and speed up improvements in Greece's capital market, the association of institutional investors came up with a series of proposals during a press conference on Tuesday.

Commenting on the bourse's current listing requirements, the association said the present status quo inhibits companies which do not show sustained profitability for three-to-five years from going public.

"It is time to expand the corporate market which is eyeing listing on the bourse. We could, for example, allow privatised, previously loss-making corporations, to be listed and raise capital," the association's president, Alexis Pilavios told reporters.
The exchange's small-cap parallel market should not be maintained in its present form as most listings satisfy requirements for the bourse's main market.

"A new parallel market could be formed, modelled after the French, Dutch and British markets where companies without the current prerequisite of three years of profitability could be listed," he said.
Pilavios said the stock market was now mature enough to introduce margin trading and short selling, measures which would improve its depth.
He said it was time to introduce floor specialists as is the practice on the New York stock exchange who would intervene to narrow bid - offer spreads when these exceed 3.0-4.0 percent.
After-hours trading based on the market's close would also help improve volumes.

Furthermore, the institutional investors association whose members include closed-end funds and mutual fund management companies thinks it is time to raise the daily volatility limits to 10 percent from the current 8.0 percent.
The recent removal of volatility limits during the three-day trade debut of new listings has been tried successfully, Pilavios said.

On the pending introduction of a derivatives market, starting with a stock index futures contract and stock options, authorities should not rush but first seek to complete share dematerialisation -- paperless settlement with the clearing house.
The Athens stock exchange should establish a market surveillance division modelled after similar operations in large exchanges abroad, he said.

And commenting on share buy-backs which under current regulations are allowed up to 10 percent, the association believes that listed companies which have bought back shares should not be allowed to sell them back to the market.

Unless these are distributed to staff via stock options they should be nulled. Corporate boards are privy to insider information and have an advantage when it comes to deciding when to sell these shares, Pilavios told reporters. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
